title: Sh-A-L
hook: sha'al, to ask; she'elah, a question

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-Ch-D: echad, one, the last word of the Shema, and the end of a week. Your line was one. Did you manage one thing at a time? A new week starts with a question. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

A woman named Hannah is praying in the sanctuary at Shiloh, so hard that her lips move but no sound comes out, and the priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't. She's asking for a child. In time she has a son, and the text gives her own explanation of his name: she "called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the LORD." In Hebrew, asked is she'iltiv, from the root sha'al. The prophet's whole life starts as an answer to someone's question. Today's root is the asking.
screen: `HANNAH PRAYS WITHOUT A SOUND.` → `A SON NAMED SAMUEL.` → `I HAVE ASKED HIM OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Sh-A-L. Shin, alef, lamed. Sha'al: to ask. She'elah: a question. Turn it three ways. First, asking after someone. When Joseph, now a ruler in Egypt, sees his brothers again, they don't yet know who he is. And when they bow to him, the text says: "he asked them of their welfare." In Hebrew, he asked them for shalom. Then he asks about their old father. In this root, asking isn't only for information. It's how you reach for someone. Second, the table. The Torah expects children to ask: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The Passover seder is built around that. The youngest asks why this night is different. The Haggadah imagines four kinds of children, and one of them doesn't know how to ask at all. For that child, it says, you open the conversation yourself. A question is so central that if it's missing, someone has to start one. Third, the library. For many centuries, when Jews had a hard question about how to live, they wrote to a rabbi, and the rabbi wrote back. Those letters are called she'elot u'teshuvot: questions and answers. Whole shelves of Jewish law grew out of people asking. In this tradition, a question isn't a sign you're lost. It's how the conversation stays alive. Hannah asked, and a prophet came. Children ask, and a story gets told. Someone writes in, and the law grows.
screen: `JOSEPH ASKS AFTER THEIR SHALOM.` · `WHAT MEAN YE BY THIS SERVICE?` · `THE CHILD WHO CAN'T ASK.` · `SHE'ELOT U'TESHUVOT: LETTERS ASKING.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION KEEPS IT ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one question. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you see often and rarely ask about. A coworker, a neighbor, someone at the next desk or the next seat. Notice what you don't know about them. Where they grew up. What their week has been like. What they're carrying. Let one question take shape, simple enough to ask out loud, the way Joseph asked after his brothers' shalom. Hold it quietly, the way Hannah held hers, lips barely moving. If you pray, you can pray for that person's shalom too. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ONE PERSON YOU SEE OFTEN.` · `ONE THING YOU DON'T KNOW.` · `SHAPE THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sh-A-L. Shin, alef, lamed: the root of sha'al, to ask, and she'elah, a question, the word inside Hannah's naming of Samuel. Today's word.
Your line: ask. Today, ask one person how they really are, the way Joseph asked his brothers, and then ask one more question about the answer. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder the youngest child traditionally asks why this night is different, and Jews bring hard questions of practice to a rabbi; the written exchanges are called she'elot u'teshuvot, questions and answers.

notes: Editor pass: practice rewritten to ask after one person, as Joseph did; the old 'question you've been carrying' practice repeated days 1396 and 1399.
1 Samuel 1:12–14 paraphrased (lips moving, no voice, Eli thinks she is drunk). 'In time' paraphrases 1:20 ('when the time was come about').
The text's explanation of Samuel's name via sha'al (she'iltiv) is the text's own; no claim is made about the name's actual linguistic origin.
Genesis 43:27 quoted from KJV; Hebrew vayish'al lahem l'shalom. Joseph's brothers do not yet recognize him (Genesis 42:8). The bow is 43:26.
Exodus 12:26 quoted from KJV. Haggadah four children paraphrased (she'eino yode'a lishol, at petach lo).
'For many centuries' and responsa (she'elot u'teshuvot) described without dates or counts. Confirm.
